newsitem.title: USA: CSCE world sugar ends sharply up, buying mixed.
newsitem.headline: CSCE world sugar ends sharply up, buying mixed.

text.p: CSCE benchmark July world sugar closed at a two-week high, buoyed by positive signals from both the fundamental and technical sides of the market, trading sources said.

Talk that Cargill may have found a buyer for nearly 360,000 tonnes of sugar, as indicated by rumors of up to 15 vessels in Brazil, gave the market an early lift, floor sources said. Other support came from talk that some of the Brazilian origin could be from the new crop.
"There are rumors flying all over the place and no one knows what's true, but they lent early support to the market," a trader said.
Speculative-type buying emerged once July steadied above 10.95 cents, where buy stops had been cited. Additional buying by the speculators emerged over 11.00 cents.
"It may have been initially trade and fundamental-inspired steadiness which spilled into technical buying by the specs," a dealer said.
July climbed to a two-week high of 11.08 cents, where producer selling emerged to block further gains. Dealers said the close over 11.00 cents in July, however, could fuel prices higher on Tuesday.
Resistance was pegged at 11.09 cents, the recent high hit on April 30, followed by 11.20 cents.
Benchmark July closed 0.16 cent firmer at 11.04 cents per lb, having ranged from 11.08 to 10.89 cents. The rest of the board settled 0.17 to 0.05 cent higher.
Volume was estimated at 25,135 lots, compared with Friday's official 8,820 lots.
Open interest in July rose 1,057 lots to 74,636 lots, as of early Friday.

In fundamental news, the U.S. Department of Agriculture approved a 200,000 tonne increase in the U.S. sugar import quota, and forecast a 1996/97 sugar stocks-to-use ratio of 15.4 percent. The ratio is a key figure in setting the import quota.

The USDA allocated 1.7 million tonnes of sugar imports at the beginning of fiscal 1997, but said adjustments would be considered during the year. A ratio of 15.5 percent or less boosts the quota by 200,000 tonnes.
